title: The Teenage Girl Who Remembers Everything - Nautilus
gist: Nautilus interviews a scientist about a 16-year-old with Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory (HSAM), a condition first clinically identified in 2006. Experts suggest perhaps no more than about 100 people worldwide have it.

insights.claim: The first clinical case of Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory (HSAM) was identified in 2006, when the condition was named.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: HSAM is a young research area, so neuroscience findings on memory mechanisms are still early-stage.
insights.quote: In 2006, the first clinical case of such a person was identified, and the condition was given a name: Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory, or HSAM.

insights.claim: Some experts propose there may be no more than about 100 people on Earth with Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Extreme rarity limits sample sizes and the pace of research into memory enhancement.
insights.quote: Some experts propose that there may be no more than 100 or so people on Earth with the condition.

insights.claim: People with HSAM can effortlessly recall mundane personal details for a given date, such as what they ate for lunch, what they wore, and the weather.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Effortless recall in rare individuals offers a natural experiment for understanding memory, relevant to neuroscience and cognitive-health research.

insights.claim: Ordinary human memory is fallible, with people routinely misremembering and forgetting life events, which makes HSAM cases scientifically notable as outliers.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Framing forgetting as normal (the article links 'Faulty Memory is a Feature not a Bug') tempers expectations for memory-enhancement products.
insights.quote: The memory is fallible. We misremember and forget the events of our lives all of the time.
